summary:
Criminal liability for sexual conduct in Niue is set by Niue's own statute law. Sections 43 and 44 of the Criminal Law Code criminalised male homosexual conduct: consensual sodomy carried up to ten years' imprisonment, attempted buggery and indecent assault on males fell under the same provisions, and indecency between males carried up to five years. The provisions were inherited from New Zealand through the 1901 annexation, retained when Niue achieved self-governance in 1974, and left untouched by New Zealand's own decriminalisation in 1986, which amended New Zealand law only (Human Dignity Trust; Wikipedia).

Those sections were repealed by the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act 2024, passed in May 2024 and in force from June 2024, decriminalising male homosexual activity (Human Dignity Trust). No source in the current inventory records criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct in Niue today, and none documents enforcement against queer people.

Relationship recognition runs the other way. Section 6 of the Family Relationships Act 2022 expressly prohibits same-sex marriage, and same-sex unions are not recognised in Niue even though they are recognised in New Zealand. Same-sex couples, and households headed by same-sex couples, are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples (Wikipedia).

New Zealand nationality and passport rules govern entry into Niue; the territory operates no independent citizenship or passport regime.
tangentialFactors:
The UN Free & Equal Pacific information sheet of August 2015 lists the fakafifine of Niue among the diverse pre-colonial Pacific gender identities, describing them as important parts of the cultural treasure of the region. A visitor should expect a locally recognised third-gender tradition alongside whatever statutory position applies to gender identity, which the current inventory does not establish.

Niue's position diverges from New Zealand's on two points that a visitor may assume are shared: New Zealand decriminalised in 1986 and recognises same-sex unions, while Niue's own code kept the offences until 2024 and its 2022 family statute bars same-sex marriage.

The age of consent was equalised in May 2011 according to ILGA State-Sponsored Homophobia, but the sex-asymmetric age of majority in the Niue Act 1966 remains on the books.
localsOnly:
Under Part 21 of the Niue Act 1966 (Marriage of Minors), the age of majority is 21 for men and 19 for women. The asymmetry has not been amended and continues to bear on marriage capacity for residents.

Section 6 of the Family Relationships Act 2022 prohibits same-sex marriage outright, so the marriage-based protections of Niue law are unavailable to same-sex couples regardless of the age-of-majority rules.

The Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act 2024 removed the male homosexual offences from the Criminal Law Code; residents are no longer exposed to liability under ss.43-44 for consensual conduct.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no source on trans-specific legal questions in Niue: change of gender markers on identity documents, legal recognition of non-binary or third-gender status, access to gender-affirming healthcare, or prohibition of discrimination on grounds of gender identity. These remain unresolved and are not sourced here.

Sources disagree on the exact date of the 2024 repeal: Human Dignity Trust records passage in May and entry into force in June, while Wikipedia records enactment on 5 June 2024. The discrepancy is unresolved.

No source in the inventory documents enforcement practice, police conduct, hate-crime incidents, or violence against trans people in Niue, and none records entry screening, facility access, or healthcare availability for trans visitors. Absence of such records is not evidence of safety.
